question.text: The illiquidity premium in AIF investing refers to:

answer.text: A penalty for investing in AIFs
The additional expected return investors demand to compensate for the inability to easily sell their investment
A fee charged by SEBI for AIF registration

explanation.text: The Logic: Category I/II AIFs are close-ended and primarily illiquid, with investors often unable to exit until winding up and distributions are completed. The workbook supports higher return expectations for unsystematic/illiquidity risk and hurdle rates meant to compensate investors for higher illiquidity and longer holding risk. The Trap: The premium is an expectation, not a guarantee. If realised returns do not exceed what comparable, more-liquid markets could have earned, the illiquidity went uncompensated. Note: Earlier wording included a 7-10 year lockup, a 3-5% annualised premium, and liquid-alternative advice. Those numeric premium and timing claims are not directly supported by the checked workbook and have been removed; only the illiquidity-compensation concept and comparable-market wording remain.
